newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Italian troops splash ashore in rebel-held Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italian troops splash ashore in rebel-held Albania.

text.p: Italian marines stormed onto the beaches of the rebel-held Albanian port city of Vlore with a mighty show of force on Monday, apparently designed to frighten off any would-be attackers.

The spectacular seaborne landing by 160 combat-ready Italian soldiers came without any warning. About 30 tanks and armoured vehicles rolled onto shore after being ferried in from a transport ship on amphibious landing craft.

They were accompanied by Italian marines in camouflage gear who leaped off their own hovercraft onto the shore. With rifles at the ready position, the soldiers immediately began searching buildings near the port.
Several of the tanks were unloaded just off the shore and moved through shoulder-high surf onto the beach.
Hovercraft and launches were everywhere in the bay after racing in from the Italian navy transport ship San Giusto.
Some 12 frogmen spilled out of the hovercraft and waded into the sea to look for submerged obsacles. One soldier in uniform plunged after them into the water.
"The operation went exactly according to plan," said Italian commanding officer Colonel Vincenzo Lops.
The troops were the first permanent contingent of soldiers into Vlore from a 6,000-strong security force that will protect the delivery of humanitarian aid to Albania's poor and needy.
Vlore, which is 150 km (90 miles) south of Tirana, is still in rebel control after an armed uprising that has since claimed more than 300 lives began in the south.
More than a thousand Albanians went to the heavily guarded dock to welcome the troops after a daily rally in the city square led by the rebel committee which controls the port.
"Our brothers, the Italians," they chanted. "We're glad our brothers have come."
Captain Fabrizio Arconi, who was in charge of a company of 100 soldiers guarding the port, told Reuters: "We're delighted with the welcome we have received."
Gunfire crackled in the distance, a daily feature of life in southern Albania, but posed no direct threat to the troops.
"The first thing is to take control of the port," Arconi said. "Today we are not going to be moving around the town. Today we are going to take control of the port and set up the barracks."
